paths.title: Frontend Performance & Core Web Experience
paths.description: Measure loading, rendering, interaction, JavaScript, images, fonts, caching, and long tasks before optimizing the user-visible bottleneck.
topics: Performance measurement
Performance work needs repeatable measurements and user-centered metrics rather than intuition about which code looks expensive.
Capture baseline lab traces and real-user metrics where available, then optimize the largest user-visible bottleneck first.
Largest Contentful Paint
LCP reflects when the largest relevant above-the-fold content is rendered and is affected by server, network, resource, and rendering delays.
Identify the actual LCP element and prioritize its document discovery, response, decoding, and rendering path.
Interaction responsiveness
Long tasks and excessive main-thread work delay user input even after a page appears loaded.
Break long synchronous work, reduce unnecessary JavaScript, and measure interaction traces instead of only bundle size.
Layout stability
Unexpected movement often comes from media without dimensions, late content, fonts, or dynamically inserted UI.
Reserve space with dimensions or aspect-ratio and avoid inserting content above what the user is already reading unless expected.
Critical resource loading
Scripts, styles, fonts, and media have different priorities and blocking behavior in the loading pipeline.
Keep critical resources discoverable, defer noncritical JavaScript, and use preload or preconnect only when trace evidence shows benefit.
JavaScript budget
JavaScript costs download, parse, compile, execute, and memory time, especially on slower devices.
Ship less code, split by user journey, remove unused dependencies, and lazy-load features that are not required for initial interaction.
Image optimization
Images are often the largest transfer cost and require correct dimensions, format, compression, responsive selection, and lazy loading.
Serve appropriately sized modern formats, include intrinsic dimensions, and avoid lazy-loading the primary above-the-fold image.
Font performance
Font files can delay text styling and cause reflow when fallback metrics differ.
Subset required glyphs, minimize families and weights, choose a font-display strategy, and tune fallbacks for layout-sensitive text.
HTTP caching
Cache-Control, validators, immutable hashed assets, and CDN behavior can avoid repeated transfer while preserving freshness.
Use content hashes for long-lived static assets and define revalidation/freshness separately for HTML and API data.
Performance regression gates
Optimizations decay when new features silently add payload, requests, long tasks, or layout shifts.
Track performance budgets in CI or monitoring and investigate regressions with traces rather than normalizing gradual slowdown.

paths.title: Media, Storage, PWA & Offline Capabilities
paths.description: Handle images, SVG, audio/video, storage, service workers, caching, installability, background behavior, and offline data deliberately.
topics: SVG usage
SVG provides scalable vector graphics that can be embedded, linked, styled, or scripted with different security and accessibility properties.
Use inline SVG when styling/interaction needs it and external image SVG when isolation and caching are more valuable.
Canvas rendering
Canvas provides an immediate-mode bitmap drawing surface that does not expose drawn content as normal DOM semantics.
Use Canvas for high-volume custom graphics and provide accessible text or interaction alternatives for meaningful content.
Audio and video
Media elements support native playback, tracks, preload strategies, posters, controls, and streaming behavior.
Provide captions/transcripts where appropriate, avoid autoplay with sound, and choose preload according to actual user intent.
Object URLs
URL.createObjectURL exposes Blob or File data through temporary URLs that retain backing resources until revoked.
Revoke object URLs when previews or downloads are no longer needed to avoid retaining large blobs in memory.
Web Storage limits
localStorage and sessionStorage are synchronous string stores and can block the main thread for large or frequent operations.
Use them for small non-sensitive preferences and use IndexedDB for larger structured offline data.
IndexedDB
IndexedDB is an asynchronous transactional browser database suited to larger structured data and indexes.
Version schemas carefully, handle upgrade transactions, and define conflict/synchronization behavior before offline writes are enabled.
Service-worker lifecycle
Service workers install, activate, and control clients independently from page lifetime, which creates update and cache-version concerns.
Use explicit cache versions, safe activation behavior, and an update UX that does not strand users on incompatible assets.
Caching strategies
Cache-first, network-first, stale-while-revalidate, and offline fallback strategies serve different resource freshness requirements.
Choose a strategy per resource class and never cache sensitive authenticated responses without a clear privacy model.
Offline mutation
Writing while offline creates synchronization, ordering, conflict, and duplicate-submission problems when connectivity returns.
Queue mutations only when operations are replay-safe and surface sync/conflict state to the user.
Installable web applications
Manifest metadata, secure serving, service-worker behavior, responsive UI, and platform conventions influence installability and app-like use.
Treat installation as an enhancement and preserve full browser usability for users who never install the application.

paths.title: Frontend Testing, Debugging & DevTools
paths.description: Combine unit, DOM/component, integration, end-to-end, visual, accessibility, network, and browser-tool evidence to verify behavior.
topics: Testing pyramid by risk
Different defects are cheapest to catch at different levels, so one test style cannot economically prove an entire frontend.
Use unit tests for pure logic, DOM/component tests for interaction, and end-to-end tests for a small set of critical user journeys.
Behavior-first assertions
Tests should observe user-visible outputs and stable contracts instead of internal implementation details.
Query elements by role/label where possible and assert rendered states, requests, navigation, or persisted effects.
Async testing
Promises, timers, rendering queues, and network mocks can make tests pass before the observable state has settled.
Wait for the condition a user would observe and avoid arbitrary sleeps that hide race conditions.
Network mocking
Mocked APIs make tests deterministic but can drift from real contracts or omit protocol behavior.
Use contract fixtures or schema validation and keep a layer of integration/e2e tests against realistic backend behavior.
End-to-end scope
E2E tests provide high confidence across layers but are slower and more sensitive to environment instability.
Cover high-value workflows, use stable selectors/roles, isolate test data, and keep failure artifacts such as screenshots and traces.
Visual regression
Screenshot comparison detects unintended layout or style changes that semantic tests may not notice.
Run visual checks on stable representative states and review intentional baseline changes rather than auto-accepting them.
Accessibility automation
Automated accessibility engines catch machine-detectable issues such as missing labels or some contrast problems.
Integrate automated checks but retain keyboard, zoom, semantic, and screen-reader testing for issues tools cannot infer.
Console and network failures
A page can look correct while producing unhandled promise rejections, failed resources, or repeated requests.
Fail tests or release checks on unexpected console errors and inspect request waterfalls for duplicate or incorrect calls.
Source-level debugging
Breakpoints, watch expressions, stack traces, source maps, and conditional pauses reveal runtime state at the failure point.
Reproduce the bug first and inspect actual values before editing code based on a guessed cause.
Performance debugging
CPU profiles, rendering tracks, memory snapshots, and network waterfalls explain slowness better than code inspection alone.
Capture a trace around the user-visible slowdown and connect long tasks, layout, memory, or requests to the specific interaction.

paths.title: Framework & Rendering Architecture
paths.description: Understand component frameworks, reactivity, virtual DOM or compiled updates, routing, SSR, hydration, islands, server components, and framework tradeoffs.
topics: Framework value proposition
Frameworks coordinate rendering, components, state, routing, data, build tooling, and conventions at the cost of abstraction and upgrade surface.
Choose a framework when its ecosystem and model reduce whole-product complexity rather than because every frontend is assumed to require one.
Reactive dependency tracking
Reactive systems update views when tracked inputs change, using runtime proxies/signals or compile-time analysis depending on the framework.
Understand what establishes a dependency and avoid side effects inside computations expected to remain pure.
Virtual DOM and diffing
Some frameworks represent UI as virtual trees and reconcile changes against prior output using identity and keys.
Use stable keys and avoid mutating state in ways the framework cannot detect or reconcile predictably.
Compiled rendering
Compilers can transform templates/components into targeted DOM operations and remove runtime abstraction cost.
Learn the generated lifecycle model so performance or state behavior is not treated as framework magic.
Client-side rendering
CSR downloads code and data before building substantial UI in the browser, enabling rich navigation but increasing client work.
Use CSR for interaction-heavy regions while controlling bundle size, startup cost, loading states, and deep-link behavior.
Server-side rendering
SSR sends useful HTML from the server before client JavaScript attaches behavior.
Use SSR when first render, crawling, or server data access benefits justify server complexity and hydration constraints.
Hydration
Hydration connects server-rendered markup to client component state and event handlers, requiring server and client output to agree.
Eliminate nondeterministic render differences and investigate hydration warnings rather than suppressing them.
Static generation and incremental regeneration
Pre-rendering can move work to build or controlled regeneration time for content that does not need request-time personalization.
Choose static output for suitably stable pages and define freshness/invalidation behavior explicitly.
Islands and partial hydration
Island architectures keep most HTML static while hydrating only interactive regions.
Use islands when independent interactive components can reduce shipped JavaScript without complicating shared state excessively.
Server/client component boundaries
Some modern frameworks allow component trees to split between server-only data work and client-interactive code.
Keep secrets and heavy server dependencies behind server boundaries and minimize client transitions to reduce payload and serialization complexity.

paths.title: Production Frontend Delivery & Operations
paths.description: Ship frontend applications with compatibility, deployment, cache safety, observability, error handling, feature flags, monitoring, and release discipline.
topics: Browser support policy
Supported browser versions and device capabilities determine which syntax, APIs, polyfills, and test environments are required.
Publish a support matrix, use compatibility data, and test representative engines instead of assuming one Chromium browser represents the web.
Production build integrity
Optimized builds may minify, split, tree-shake, hash, transform, and inject environment-specific configuration.
Test the actual production build locally or in preview and verify that build-time variables expose no secrets.
Asset versioning
Hashed immutable assets can be cached long-term while HTML or manifests need freshness so they reference current assets.
Use content-hashed filenames and deployment strategies that avoid deleting assets still referenced by clients with older HTML.
Atomic deployment
Users should not receive a mixture of incompatible old and new application files during rollout.
Publish versioned assets before switching entry documents and keep rollback artifacts available until the release is proven healthy.
Client error reporting
Unhandled exceptions and rejected promises should produce diagnosable telemetry without exposing sensitive user data.
Capture errors with release/version context, stack traces and breadcrumbs while redacting credentials, personal data, and request bodies as needed.
Frontend observability
Real-user metrics reveal performance, errors, route health, and device conditions that lab testing cannot fully reproduce.
Instrument important user journeys with privacy-conscious metrics and correlate regressions to deployments.
Feature flags
Flags separate deployment from release but add configuration states that must be tested, owned, and removed.
Define defaults and targeting centrally, test both paths where risk warrants it, and delete stale flags after rollout.
Graceful degradation
Analytics, personalization, secondary APIs, and noncritical widgets can fail without making core product actions unusable.
Isolate optional integrations and design failure boundaries so critical content and actions remain available.
Release verification
A green build does not prove CDN behavior, headers, routes, auth redirects, cache state, or real production integrations.
Run post-deploy smoke tests on critical routes and inspect console, network, security headers, and monitoring after release.
Frontend ownership
Production quality requires clear owners for accessibility, performance, dependencies, incidents, browser support, and shared components.
Maintain runbooks and review recurring telemetry so quality work is continuous rather than a pre-launch cleanup phase.
